column2: The group sits down; Ma Peak appears, points to the Indian woman, and refuses to serve her; Dan Rice objects that she is from India; Ma Peak folds her arms and digs in; Olson takes her aside, deploys his powers of persuasion, and fails; they order beers to go and return to the college. Words: “I kin serve evahbody but you” / “But she's from India” / “Look at 'er, black as a nigger” / “Git 'er outa here!” Atmosphere: Heat, the group's stunned embarrassment, helplessness before the law Stakes: The college's bubble bursts: even Olson's charm can do nothing against legal racism.

After two sets at the Blue Note, their money gone, the group heads for the Mercedes; through the window, Holiday glimpsed on her break, a gardenia in her hair, gin and a Slim Jim; they go in, the women shyly taking a booth; Rumaker goes to the bar, heart pounding; she teases him (“college boy?”) and regrets not knowing the words to “My Funny Valentine”; a quarter in the jukebox; she stands behind him and says “Sing”; he starts, she takes over and sings into his right ear; he stands transfixed. Words: “You a college boy?”; “I've had heartburn all day and haven't eaten a thing—Gimme one of them Slim Jims”; “You know the words?”; “Sing” Atmosphere: Snow outside, an empty, drab bar, gin and spicy jerky, a furtive and magical intimacy Stakes: The idol humanized in an ordinary place, an echo of the failed poem of long ago, the revenge of writing to come.

Cornelia, in her Sunday clothes, waits in front of the dining hall; Rumaker invites her into the front; she refuses, laughing, “Naw, naw, naw,” and climbs into the back; Rumaker jokes without understanding; Mary says nothing; she has understood; Cornelia is dropped off in her Black neighborhood. Words: “Don't be silly, Cornelia… there's plenty room” / “Naw, naw, naw… I'll be perfectly fine back here” Atmosphere: A sunny Sunday, naive good humor on one side, caution on the other Stakes: Segregation intrudes even into kindness; Rumaker understands too late.

After days of approach (visits to the study), they head for the Quiet House; Bill's eyes ashamed of desire; the door shut, total darkness, mutual hunger; a damp bench; further meetings at the Quiet House or in the study; Bill leaves, and Rumaker misses him. Atmosphere: Damp, mildew, total darkness, the warmth of bodies in the cold Stakes: Desire and guilt in a desecrated memorial, with Merrill still in Houston in the background.

Rumaker leaves South Lodge for his study and spots the crouching figure spying on the lighted bathroom; he recognizes Alvin and passes silently, both of them in the shadows, toward the Studies Building. Atmosphere: Night, complicit shadows Stakes: Two hidden sexualities brush past each other without seeing each other, a mirror of Rumaker's homosexuality.

Arrived from Stuttgart, the large pale blue volumes with the big black brushstroke O; Olson, calm, looks at the copy he is holding, then at the students, without a word, his joy plain to see; the poorest scrape together the three dollars by saving on food and beer. Atmosphere: A bright afternoon, excited silence, shared recognition Stakes: The master becomes a book; the fragile consecration of a dying college

Rumaker has hidden the suitcase under the bed; he gets up without a sound, dresses in the dark, passes the Gatehouse, and walks down the mountain to the county road to hitchhike; inwardly he turns back toward Merrill, whom he believes relieved to see him go Atmosphere: Predawn darkness, silent birds, a heavy chest, heart and mind as black as the night Stakes: Fleeing to survive; a violent desire to stay one last time

Sitting cross-legged on the rice mat, Rumaker unburdens himself of his story with Merrill; Mary Ann listens sympathetically, to the point of weariness Atmosphere: The poor, warm intimacy of the single room Stakes: The gradual healing of the obsession

The Montana potter teaches for three weeks and becomes friends with the Cage/Cunningham circle; a photograph of him taken at Mrs. Ira Julian's on the way to New York; then a first trip to New York with Richards and Tudor Words: “I enjoyed it because I'd never been exposed to anything like they had there... It was so beautiful and so new to me” Atmosphere: A craftsman dazzled by the avant-garde Stakes: A functional potter's swing toward the revolution of clay sculpture

At the end of the summer of 1953, after six weeks of work with the seven dancers from New York, the brand-new company presents its first programs: four new works, including Banjo (Cunningham traces a circle around the stage while three dancers move in unison), Dime a Dance, Septet (four dancers in multifigure poses, in almost constant contact yet autonomous), and Untitled Solo. Atmosphere: A room without a proscenium, dancers scattered in separate spaces, a joint feeling of singular efforts and cooperation. Stakes: The birth of a legend: Black Mountain as the matrix of the Cunningham company.

After a Florentine exhibition in which his works are shown, a hostile critic disparages them; Rauschenberg follows his advice and throws them into the Arno. Words: The critic reportedly advised getting rid of them. Atmosphere: A gesture of temper and wounded pride, by the river. Stakes: The young artist's dramatic break with his European works.

The young Rauschenberg explains his project: erasing a well-known drawing. De Kooning, worried but intrigued, goes through his works, sets aside worthless sketches, and chooses a drawing covered with grease crayon, grease pencil, ink, and pencil, beautiful enough to be missed and tough enough to resist the eraser. Rauschenberg takes the sheet away and will spend nearly a month erasing it. Words: De Kooning understands that his contribution must not be an insignificant sketch but a drawing whose loss he will feel Atmosphere: Tension mixed with irony: an elder entrusts his work to a young man who announces he wants to destroy it Stakes: Can erasure be a work? Can a gift be an accepted loss?

Cage drives the car whose coated tire leaves its print on the paper assembled by Rauschenberg; then each claims the work. Words: Rauschenberg: Cage did a fine job, but he considers it his print. Cage, good-naturedly, asks which of the two of them drove the car. Atmosphere: Friendly sparring Stakes: Who is the author, the conceiver or the executor?

The disgusted critic suggests throwing the meditative boxes and personal fetishes into the Arno; when the exhibition closes, Rauschenberg, weighting the boxes so they will never resurface, throws them in as ordered. Words: The critic's suggestion: throw them into the Arno Atmosphere: Scandal, a spectacular and deliberate gesture Stakes: Absorbing the hostile enemy into the work; turning insult into performance

One quiet Sunday morning, Rauschenberg glues twenty sheets into a 22-foot strip; he coats the rear tire of Cage's Model A with black house paint; Cage drives slowly, and the tire prints the strip of paper Atmosphere: Sunday calm, serious play among friends Stakes: Painting as the trace of a shared event

With very few students enrolled, the whole college moves up the hill to the faculty cottages, abandoning the lower campus. Atmosphere: Fall 1953, renunciation Stakes: The physical shrinking of the dream

Day after day, from morning into the night, the dancers work with Cunningham eight hours or more; Arnold Eagle photographs the Untitled Solo; Cunningham takes his choreographic notes. Words: dancing from morning to night seemed “right” Atmosphere: Total immersion, art, life, and process Stakes: A life redirected by the intensity of the work

Goodman moves to a new place; his friends gather to paint the apartment; the walls hold original paintings they have given him. Atmosphere: Community warmth, the solidarity of decent poverty Stakes: Giving material form to the mutual aid Goodman preaches

The young Rauschenberg, 28, asks de Kooning, 49, for a drawing, announcing his intention to erase it; the master does not object and chooses an ink drawing with traces of pencil; Rauschenberg erases for a month before declaring the work his own. Words: Rauschenberg (1953): it was nothing destructive; he un-drew the drawing with the eraser on the end of his pencil. Stakes: The filial and iconoclastic gesture of a new generation toward the master, at the very moment of his consecration

Two weeks after his promise, Albers receives Elaine: everywhere, small paintings on paper, a square within a square of another color, which he names before her eyes. During the interview and Rudy's photographs, the painter starts chasing the critic around the table to kiss her. Words: Albers: “I will make some paintings that express my color philosophy”; “I will call this series 'Homage to the Square'”. Atmosphere: A living room with no studio, the photographer's laughter, a gallant comedy. Stakes: The public christening of a major series, captured by the critic and the lens.

Between interviews and photographs, the trio heads for the charming neighborhood bar: smoked eel, one boilermaker after another. When the article is delivered, Diller, delighted by the offered review, passes on Rose Fried's warning; Elaine laughs, flattered. At their last meeting, he hides his grimaces of pain. Words: Rose Fried (as reported by Diller): “Watch out for that Elaine de Kooning. She's one smart cookie and she's out to cut your throat” Atmosphere: The weary charm of a Fitzgerald couple, good food, elegant drinking, pain dully hidden. Stakes: A portrait of the artist as a doomed gentleman.

Delivery of two books on the nude; an immediate craving for the collection of photographs; ribald and worldly comparisons between painters and photographs; then a more sustained reading of the book of paintings. Words: Reflections that the Renaissance counterpart of Christine Jorgensen could have posed for many painters Atmosphere: Sunny, relaxed, a mocking and free parlor Stakes: The artists' male gaze on the female body, held up to ridicule by the author
For an evening of poets' plays, Elaine designs the sets for Schuyler's short play in three days on a seventeen-dollar budget; she did them for fourteen and had a good meal with the three left over.

After tearing apart at length Rumaker's text about his old deceitful Irish landlady, Olson starts attacking Rumaker himself, telling him in substance that he cannot help him because he does not love him. Rumaker, defenseless, shrinks under the gaze of the other students, half pity, half contempt. It is the first time Olson has been so furious with him, worse than his screeds on his manuscripts. A sunny afternoon, pines and valley visible through the wide windows; Rumaker head down, feeling he can no longer breathe Consequences: In retrospect Rumaker sees it as a second birth, the beginning of his life as a writer and of his true integration into the college; he becomes attached to Olson as to a second spiritual father

That same evening, Rumaker, too stunned to speak or eat, dares not sit at Olson's table; Olson is a few tables away, his brow still marked with anger; students from his class look at him, perhaps talk about him. Rumaker steals a glance at Olson, who catches him at it and keeps his furious frown
Having fallen ill, he leaves North Africa for Italy.

Myers announces three days and seventeen dollars for the sets of Presenting Jane; Elaine delivers them for fourteen and feasts on the remaining three Words: She made the sets for fourteen and had a good meal with the three left over Atmosphere: The euphoric resourcefulness of the poets' world Stakes: Living art on a pittance

Olson first tears apart at length the text about the Irish landlady, then turns on Rumaker himself; Rumaker shrinks, speechless, feels skinless; the others stare at him, pity in some, contempt in others. Words: Olson: “I can't help you because I don't love you” Atmosphere: A bright afternoon in the pines, annihilated; Rumaker shrinks, barely breathing Stakes: The fear of being thrown out once again, by the man he most wants to please, and in retrospect a second birth

A shortened three-week winter institute devoted to mythology and archaeology. Olson had invited Jung himself, kept away by illness; von Franz, his closest associate at the C. G. Jung Institute in Zurich, comes in his place for several days from mid-March. Olson has been preparing the students for weeks with classes and discussions on Jung; all the Jungian material in the library and on campus passes from hand to hand Consequences: Von Franz's visit energizes the work and discussions at the college for months, even years

Hess defuses the shock: the Woman's smile is not aggressive but detached, with a touching irony and humanity; he describes the canvas as a montage of discontinuous passages (paint on papers pasted on and then removed) and notes that de Kooning credits Elaine with having put this montage effect into words. Woman I: enormous dark eyes, a sour, toothy smile, breasts like boulders, an arm shaped like a leg, pink feet in espadrilles

Von Franz, sent by the ailing Jung while she was already on a lecture tour in the United States, arrives in the late afternoon. She is taken to her room at Streamside; she comes back down to the kitchen to ask the dinner hour, then sets off at once to climb one of the Seven Sisters behind North Lodge, steep, a half-hour climb with no preamble. A plain blouse, a dark wool jacket, a gray wool skirt, sturdy brown hiking shoes, lightly waved gray hair; she comes back exactly half an hour later, at the stroke of Cornelia's gong, chubby-cheeked and cheerful Consequences: Rumaker likes her immediately, attributing her ease in the mountains to her Alpine upbringing

On Olson's advice, Rumaker, intimidated, makes an appointment to show her his recent dreams. Von Franz reads quickly, concentrated, with little nods and gurgles, interpreting too fast for him to follow, his heart pounding in his ears. She identifies in his dream of Olson in a black robe and turban the archetype of the Wise Old Man to whom he must give himself. Each person is allowed only a limited number of minutes, so many come “clutching our dreams.” A small pine-paneled room, fading light on the mountains through the window; steel-rimmed glasses; rough wooden steps up to the attic, which Rumaker compares to the marble stairs of the sibyl's temple Consequences: The interpretation of the Wise Old Man confirms Rumaker in his resolve to give himself over to Olson; a feeling of deep and lasting communion

Wes directs almost the whole school in Brecht's Mother Courage, with Rumaker doing the lighting. Cynthia Homire plays Mother Courage; Fee Dawson, with some resistance, plays the airplane pilot. After von Franz's first talk, during a question-and-answer session, Dawson brings up his role; she answers with a mischievous air that the young pilot in a blue uniform is one of her archetypes, an animus of her shadow that could lead her away from her true path. A greasy braid down Cynthia's back under her worn Levi jacket; a “roguish twinkle” in von Franz's eye

A photograph of a torn poster proclaiming “Stalin é morto”; it must therefore have been taken shortly after March 5, 1953; it documents the reconstruction policies of postwar Italy A torn poster, “Stalin é morto”
Bowles leaves Tangier for a month in Tetouan, capital of the Spanish zone; Rauschenberg stays on the same street as their hotel, Rue General Franco. Rue General Franco; Bowles's monthlong stay

A photograph by Rauschenberg showing Stalin can be dated between Stalin's death (March 5, 1953) and Rauschenberg's return to America in April 1953. Stalin died March 5, 1953; return to America in April 1953

Ferber confides to Bill that he feels sorry for Elaine; Hartigan identifies a woman from the group in each canvas; students see bullet holes, rubies from Harper's Bazaar; the press cries ugliness and sexual violence Words: Hartigan points out which one is Bill's interlocutor, which one is herself, which one is Jane Freilicher; Ferber says he is sorry for Elaine Atmosphere: Joyful scandal, Bill flattered at having shocked the avant-garde Stakes: Elaine exposed as a muse against her will

As soon as she is settled at Streamside, she comes back down to the kitchen to ask when supper is served; learning that there is half an hour left, she nods curtly, goes out the back door, crosses the road, and climbs a Seven Sister steeply until she disappears into the trees; she comes back right at the stroke of the gong, chubby-cheeked and glowing. Words: she feels refreshed, the mountains are beautiful, and she is ready to eat Atmosphere: Late afternoon, an upright, determined gait, no fuss Stakes: An immediate revelation of the visitor's character; Rumaker is smitten

Heart pounding, Rumaker climbs the wooden steps; von Franz reads his dreams quickly, all business, nods and gurgles, interpretations too quick for the ear; she recognizes the anima in his dreams and identifies Olson's black turban with the Wise Old Man; Rumaker dares not ask the big questions: is he on the wrong path? Is his queer side a false way? What is the Secret of the Golden Flower? Words: he must give himself to the Wise Old Man, who has much to teach Atmosphere: Fading light on the mountains, heartbeats in his ears, a sanctuary Stakes: Confirmation of the path: giving himself over to Olson

Following a local critic's advice, Rauschenberg throws most of the small boxes shown in Rome and Florence into the river Words: It saved him the problem of packing Atmosphere: A Dada gesture, quiet irony Stakes: The artist's relation to his works and to the market

Visiting Kline during spring vacation from BMC, Dawson is introduced to DeKooning; learning that he comes from Black Mountain, DeKooning says he was there in 1948 and starts talking about Olson and his book on Melville, with an eager, impatient “yes yes.” A handshake barely exchanged. Consequences: Proof of the intuitive harmony between BMC and New York.

De Kooning shows his paintings of women for the first time; a clamor of praise in the media, veneration in the 10th Street art world because he had paid his dues, but no one imitated these works, including the Marilyn series: the female figure remained taboo. The Marilyn series cited; East 10th Street as the heart of the art world Consequences: No imitations: woman remains a forbidden subject in abstraction

Charley Egan's gallery shows four men (Franz Kline, Philip Pavia, Jack Tworkov, George McNeil) at the Woman's College in Greensboro; they come down for a few days, then cross the state to visit Black Mountain. For Dawson these days are paradise: he had admired in Time a watercolor by Pavia made in Italy for a Container Corporation ad; they admire his new drawings of girls; they talk, drink, and play softball. Container Corporation ad in Time magazine, a watercolor by Pavia Consequences: A feeling of triumph: Black Mountain has become two schools, that of New York and the men from up north, and Charley's

J. P. Grady usually umpires but plays right field; Egan umpires. Olson at first base, Joel pitching, Franz at second, Dawson (shortstop or left field?), Dan at third: his throw to first is so hard that it sails over Egan's hands and ends up in the rhododendrons by the lake; Dan throws down his glove. Jorge in center. Dawson strikes Jonathan out at will, announcing that he is going to strike him out; Jonathan: “Pitch the ball, citizen. Don't lecture me.” Franz misses a pitch, diving like a swimmer, and Egan laughs. A glove thrown to the ground; rhododendrons by the lake

They all climb into McNeil's station wagon; Franz and Charley lower the tailgate and sit with their legs dangling. Dawson shakes Franz's hand; their eyes meet: “Write me.” “I will.” Egan, in a baseball cap, the very picture of an umpire: “Good meeting you, Fee.” The car pulls slowly away on the rutted road; Dawson walks, then runs; Franz and Egan pat the space between them: “C'mon Fee, get on. Come with us —”. He runs but stays; they wave as they turn onto the asphalt. McNeil's station wagon; a rutted dirt road; a bungalow near the white fence; the ball field and tennis court

Dawson writes to Franz asking to sleep at the back of his loft during spring vacation; Franz agrees. Dawson has to cut it short: a hearing in late April before a judge in Asheville; his conscientious objection is rejected, he is classified 1-A, off to the army. Late April 1953; classification 1-A Consequences: At the end of July 1953, the Korean armistice is signed: relief, but lingering fear and anxiety, an acute sense of losing beloved places, the luminous circles
In late April, Dawson has a hearing with a judge: his protest is rejected; he is classified 1-A and will go into the army. Consequences: Imminent induction; anxiety and an acute sense of loss

The handshake barely exchanged, Kline mentions the spring vacation from Black Mountain; DeKooning says he was there in 1948; the conversation jumps to Olson: has Dawson read the book on Melville? Not yet, but he will; DeKooning's impatient “yes yes” says everything by tone alone. Words: DeKooning asks whether he has read the book on Melville; yes, yes. Atmosphere: Eagerness, an intuitive zone touched, the detail missing but the tone enough. Stakes: Living proof of the invisible link between BMC and the New York School.

Handshakes at the tailgate; the car starts off on the rutted track; Dawson walks, then runs; Franz and Egan pat the space between them; the car reaches the asphalt and disappears; Dawson waves Words: “Write me.” / “I will.” / “Good meeting you, Fee.” / “C'mon Fee, get on. Come with us —” Atmosphere: Shouted goodbyes, dust, a slow road, a breathless run Stakes: The choice to stay in a world that is ending rather than follow New York

In the spring and early summer of 1953, letters (and long-distance calls from the pay phone in the hall of the Studies Building) are no longer enough: Merrill decides to go in person to persuade Herb to leave his sick father and the family garage and come back. Rumaker secretly hopes he will fail. Expensive long-distance calls from the Studies hall; Merrill calls Herb's filial piety “gutless” Consequences: Rumaker realizes (but refuses to admit) that he is only an interim convenience for Merrill

Lodged in a residence on the Plaza de Armas, Albers is accompanied on foot by Piwonka to and from the Casa Central. He takes notes and makes drawings for future classes; not much interested in talking about the Bauhaus, he asks questions about everyday design situations: a plaza sweeper working harmoniously with a long palm frond, interlocking metal rings protecting the lawns, a mason carefully setting a glass case against a rough stone wall, a contrast that delights him. A broom made of a palm branch; translucent glass against rough stone

In an austere school, the class begins at 2:30 p.m. Albers teaches in English with simultaneous translation by León Rodríguez (who graduated in architecture that year), assisted by Piwonka. Few first-year students know the Bauhaus; some advanced students and teachers join voluntarily. The dominant local modern reference: Le Corbusier. 2:30 p.m., fourth floor above the ground floor

Albers writes his name in calligraphic cursive, asks two or three people to do the same, then copies his name exactly, upside down; no one can follow him. The point: to show that everyone writes automatically in a preset way and does not really draw.

On weekends, the Alberses travel by car with some of the teachers (a photograph with Beatriz Antoncich, Sergio Larraín, the Pérez de Arces). Josef photographs adobe colonial architecture (the church of Los Dominicos) and published pre-Columbian textiles, probably for Anni, trained in textiles at the Bauhaus. Photographs kept at The Josef and Anni Albers Foundation
In the early 1990s, Rumaker reads in The Advocate that Herlihy has died, a suicide, with no reason given Announcement in the national gay and lesbian magazine The Advocate

Below the Studies Building, line drawing in pencil on large sheets bought at Carroll Williams's college store, with nude models. Vicente goes from student to student, standing, dignified, really examining the work, with brief comments, often curt but sometimes complimentary. Large sheets of sketch paper; Vicente barely touching Rumaker's sketch for the first time Consequences: Vicente's first compliment to Rumaker, who feels taller for it
Usually very shy, she reveals an exhibitionist streak that surprises Rumaker; Bea Huss, just as reserved, poses nude on another occasion.

One morning he walks through the double doors of the theater room in nothing but a jockstrap to pose; Rumaker notes the unspoken rule of the anatomical double standard, even at Black Mountain, where the size of the phallus remains a mystery protected in public. A long, pale, finely muscled physique, a pleasure to draw

In midmorning, with a shy smile and mischief in her blue eyes, she comes in wearing a dark blue velvet robe and takes it off without hesitation, revealing an opulent Rubens body; Rumaker, who has taken her classes (metaphysical poetry in the fall, Henry James's stories in the spring), is unsettled to see her naked. Honey skin the color of her bobbed hair Consequences: Her figure instantly seduces Rumaker's pencil

Shortly before leaving the college, Harrison, always on the cutting edge, finds 33 rpm LPs of Alban Berg's Wozzeck and Lulu and plays Lulu one evening on a portable phonograph to a small, select group of regular students and summer visitors: “only those who are truly interested.” A chatty, motherly blonde, who has come in search of a cultural veneer, knits argyle through the whole opera. A revelatory discovery for Rumaker, despite the small speaker and Lou's squeaky, ecstatic commentary, sitting cross-legged by the phonograph.

Wolpe's first wife arrives with her present husband, Hans Rademacher, a mathematician formerly at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. Severe, gray, bespectacled, with a strong German voice, she practices Beethoven for hours on the dining hall Steinway with a mechanical, furious attack, technically perfect but spiritually empty in Rumaker's view; she shrieks at the slightest clink of dishes. Consequences: Rumaker, on kitchen and dining hall duty, works in silence around her

Preparing his Mozart concert in the darkened dining hall, Tudor (a chain-smoker, usually gentle) stumbles over a passage, then comes to the service window, his face tense and pale with anger, eyes shining behind his rimmed glasses, and shouts at them to be quiet before going back and throwing himself at his Steinway. A stunned silence (no one had ever silenced the kitchen's night crew), then softer conversation, then rising noise. Tudor repeats the passage, slams the keyboard lid, bangs shut the sliding pass-through window, starts again more weakly, makes mistakes, and gives up for the night, probably heading back through the woods to the isolated Music House, with no electricity, just big enough for a Steinway. Barred owls and whippoorwills in the pines as the only rival sounds at the Music House Consequences: General rumor: he should have shut the window from the start
Later that summer, he plays Webern's brief, spare compositions in concert, a first for Rumaker.

Irma's protégé, taciturn, thick-shouldered, with a mousy brown crew cut and big intense eyes, surprises everyone by playing Boulez's Second Sonata with a sensitivity that grips the audience; they even ignore the bats flying low. In contrast with Irma's mechanical Beethoven, his interpretation has the raw surge and disordered energy of the sea. Olson, overwhelmed, stands at the end and exclaims “He has soul”; the young man, shyly beaming, bows from the piano bench. Consequences: Heartfelt applause

The summer's string trio plays classical and contemporary music (Schoenberg, Webern, Stravinsky, Morton Feldman). The cellist Seymour Barab, stylish and handsome, very blond and very blue-eyed, from Chicago and living in Greenwich Village, catches Mary Ann Fretz's eye; within a year he will become her lover, then her husband. Consequences: Barab will play a peripheral role in Rumaker's life through his friend the composer Ben Weber, also from Chicago

Olson corresponds with Boulez (since Tudor played the Second Sonata in 1951) to invite him from Paris to a future institute. One Saturday afternoon at Ma Peak's, after a work detail, he spreads out on the table the letter received that day, in French and in a minuscule hand; everyone tries to decipher it, and everyone gives up in frustration; Rumaker relishes seeing Charles get a taste of his own medicine in the face of illegible handwriting. Ales drunk after a work detail; microscopic handwriting requiring a magnifying glass

Walking with Connie, Olson stops Rumaker, who is studying French with Flola, and asks him the meaning of “manqué.” Nervous, too eager to please the master, Rumaker answers “mistaken”; Charles accepts it, but the right translation would have been “failed” or “would-be.” Rumaker berates himself for days, afraid of being taken for a fool.
Years later, after giving up alcohol and drugs, desperately poor, he has to sell his first copy of Maximus, and later the second (Maximus 11-22, 1956). He still regrets them.

The poor students put together three dollars each to buy Olson's first Maximus, printed by Jonathan Williams; Rumaker saves on food and beer. Olson looks at them without a word, visibly happy. Three dollars a volume; savings made on food and beer money; a moment in full sunlight Consequences: Owning a book that became precious, later sold with regret

Years later, after giving up alcohol and drugs, desperately poor, Rumaker has to sell his first Maximus, and later the second, Maximus 11-22 of 1956. The first Maximus and Maximus 11-22 (1956) Consequences: He still misses these books

The campus buzzes one morning: a student, a former Marine, married, with one child and a second on the way, was said to have been gotten drunk and bedded in his study by a persistent visitor, rather plump and effeminate, officially there for the music program. Married, one kid and another on the way

While Merrill is away in Houston, Rumaker shows two visitors from Emory (Atlanta) around the campus. The pre-med student, with jet-black hair and beautiful black-lashed eyes, asks to see his study; his friend slips away; they kiss without a word, undress, and make love on the pallet against the wall. A pallet covered with the handwoven throw that once draped the dining hall Steinway; Kline-like black and white walls painted by Merrill Consequences: A rare happiness for the solitary Rumaker; the throw never returned to Wolpe

Albers has the students and teachers draw a jacket hanging carelessly; he examines the drawings, finds almost all of them bad, and points out the folds and imperceptible details no one has seen Words: “Ustedes no han visto que aquí hay un doblez… un pliegue y una serie de cosas que parecían imperceptibles” Atmosphere: An austere room on the fourth floor, class at 2:30 p.m., simultaneous translation from English Stakes: Drawing actual vision, not the preconceived idea

While walking, Albers notices three scenes: a sweeper harmoniously sweeping leaves with a long palm branch; interlocking metal rings protecting the lawns; a mason carefully setting a glass case against a rough stone wall; and he comments enthusiastically on the richness of the contrast between translucent glass and rough stone Words: He comments on the richness of the contrast between the translucent fragility of the glass and the roughness of the stone Atmosphere: A daily walk, morning, Albers taking notes and making sketches along the way Stakes: Albers refuses to talk about the Bauhaus: his whole attention is on the present

At 2:30 p.m., Albers writes his name on the board in calligraphic letters and asks two or three people to do the same; then he copies his own name exactly, but upside down; when he asks the students to do the same, no one can. Atmosphere: An austere room; a class in English translated by the interpreter León Rodríguez. Stakes: A demonstration that writing is convention and automatism: this class will not be conventional drawing.

Albers has them draw a carelessly hung jacket; looking at the drawings shown to him, he judges them mediocre and points out folds and imperceptible details; the students had drawn their idea of the jacket, not what they actually saw. Words: They had not noticed that there was a fold here, and a number of things that seemed imperceptible. Stakes: The gap between the idea and actual sight: the heart of Albers's teaching.

In midmorning, with a shy smile and mischief in her eyes, she walks through the double doors in a dark blue velvet robe and takes it off without hesitation, revealing a magnificent Rubens body; Rumaker, used to her as a fully clothed teacher of James and the metaphysicals, is unsettled, then his hand is literally seduced by the figure; Vicente stops at his easel for the first time and compliments the sketch. Words: Vicente compliments Rumaker's drawing for the first time Atmosphere: Dazzlement, bated breath, exhilaration Stakes: The reversal of the teacher-student relation into desired body and draftsman; Rumaker's first artistic recognition

On a portable phonograph, Lou plays Lulu for a small, select group (“only those who are truly interested”); crouched by the machine, he punctuates the music with ecstatic grimaces and squeaky comments; a motherly, chatty blonde, who has come in search of cultural uplift, knits argyle through the whole opera; despite the small speaker, a revelation for Rumaker, who had never heard Berg. Words: Lou: “only those who are truly interested” Atmosphere: Electrified intimacy, Lou's ecstasy, the visitor's indifferent knitting Stakes: The passing on of a new music, a laughing musical elitism

Tudor works on his Mozart in the darkened dining hall; the crew, beery and noisy, chatters under the pot rack; after botching a passage several times, Tudor appears at the window, shouting at them to be quiet, then throws himself back at his Steinway; a stunned silence, a gentle resumption, then the din rises again; the lid slams, the sliding window bangs shut; another, weaker attempt, cascading mistakes, final surrender, and a quiet exit into the night. Words: Tudor shouts at the crew to shut up; the crew: “How dare he!” Atmosphere: Darkness, beer, laughter, muffled anger, then silent defeat Stakes: The gentlest musician on campus against the sacred tradition of nighttime chatter, and the musician loses

At the Saturday night concert, the taciturn young pianist plays Boulez's Second Sonata with an intensity that captivates everyone, bats included; at the end, Olson stands up, overwhelmed, and exclaims his verdict; the young man, shyly beaming, thanks them from the piano bench amid heartfelt applause. Words: Olson: “He has soul” Atmosphere: Contained, then released emotion, the communion of the audience Stakes: Living sensitivity against Irma's mechanical technique, a victory of breath over the machine

After a work detail, over ales, Olson spreads out the letter received that day from Boulez, in French in a minuscule hand; everyone takes a turn at deciphering it, and Rumaker trots out his “spotty French”; they give up in frustration, a magnifying glass being needed; Rumaker inwardly relishes seeing Charles afflicted with the same trouble as his own giant, indecipherable handwriting. Atmosphere: A convivial huddle, a group game, final frustration Stakes: The distance between Paris and the mountain reduced to illegible handwriting

A tour of the campus; the young man asks to see the study; his friend disappears; the door closed; a silent embrace; clothes off; the pallet against the wall covered with the Steinway throw, against black and white walls painted by Merrill Words: None; everything is done by signs and looks Atmosphere: Rumaker's pounding heart, disbelief at his luck, weeks of abstinence Stakes: A rare consolation during Merrill's absence

Two months in Chile, one in Peru. Josef teaches at the Catholic University in Santiago and at the National School of Engineers in Lima, where he meets Fernando Belaúnde Terry, future president and editor of El Arquitecto Peruano (special issue, Sept.-Oct. 1953). Visits to Ollantaytambo, Machu Picchu, Arequipa, Pachacamac, Cuzco, Trujillo, Pisac, Cajamarquilla. After meeting Max Bill in Lima, Josef agrees to teach at Ulm (November 24, 1953–January 23, 1954), his first return to Germany since the war. Letter from Anni to Gropius of March 4, 1954

Two months in Chile (he teaches at the Universidad Católica; contact Alberto Piwonka), a month in Peru, hoped for for years; he teaches at the Escuela Nacional de Ingenieros in Lima; he meets the architect and future Peruvian president Fernando Belaúnde Terry, whose magazine El Arquitecto Peruano devotes an issue to Josef (Sept.-Oct.). He meets Max Bill in Lima; an invitation accepted: he teaches for two months at the HfG Ulm (November 24, 1953–January 23, 1954), his first return to Germany since the war. Letter from Anni to Gropius of March 4, 1954

Josef Albers, accompanied by his wife Anni, arrives in Chile to teach first-year pre-architecture students for about a month and a half, twelve hours a week. Twelve hours of class a week for about six weeks.

Four years after their first meeting (July 1949), Olson, sitting on the steps, watches Dawson walk down the road toward St. Louis to be inducted: indifferent, while Dawson is scared to death. Four straight years of closeness

At the end of July, the Korean armistice is signed; Dawson is relieved (“Whew!”) but still frightened and anxious, shot through with moments of power: his anguish at leaving beloved places is a true, heightened sense of loss, the places, the luminous circles.

Alfredo Linder, a young architect, son of Paul Linder (a fellow student of the Alberses at the Weimar Bauhaus), shows them around the museum in Lima. Before one of the world's best collections of ancient Andean textiles, Anni and Josef tell each other that, deep down, they are not alone. Subtle color, geometric designs, learned textile structures Consequences: Confirmation of the couple's chosen, sometimes solitary, artistic path

The young architect Alfredo Linder, son of Paul Linder (a former fellow student of the Alberses at the Weimar Bauhaus), guides the couple through the Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology in Lima. Anni at last stands before one of the finest collections of ancient Andean textiles; the subtle colors, geometric patterns, and textile structures confirm the couple's artistic path, and they tell each other with quiet assurance: “See, we are not alone after all”. Linder keeps a vivid memory of the scene; a sentence spoken in a low voice between Anni and Josef Consequences: An affirmation of the couple's deep bond with ancient cultures in which creativity and invention are buried values

At the end of the Summer Institute, waiting for her taxi to the station beside her expensive luggage, the young woman tells Rumaker in a curt, severe voice that he is dishonest, two-faced, and neurotic and should do something about it Expensive luggage, a taxi to the station; Rumaker relieved to see her and her shoulders disappear into the cab
Letter from Lanier to Morley of September 15, 1953, Morley's reply of September 21, letter from Wildenhain to Lanier of August 17, 1953.

The young architect Alfredo Linder, son of a fellow Bauhaus student, guides the Alberses through the museum; before the Andean textiles, the couple feels a serene satisfaction: these works confirm that their artistic path, sometimes a lonely one, is the right one. Words: They tell each other: “See, we are not alone after all”. Atmosphere: Serenity and intensity of feeling Stakes: A posthumous recognition of a lineage: the Andean weavers as peers

The young guide leads the couple through the collections; Anni finds herself face to face with the Andean textiles she had dreamed of since the Bauhaus; subtle colors, geometric patterns, structures understood from the inside; husband and wife tell each other in low voices that they are not alone on their artistic path after all Words: “See, we are not alone after all” Atmosphere: Quiet assurance, intense feeling; artistic recognition Stakes: A retrospective consecration of the couple's solitary path

After the Summer Institute ends, she waits for her taxi to the station amid her expensive luggage; in her brittle voice, she delivers her parting diagnosis; Rumaker, relieved, watches her get into the cab Words: Michael is dishonest, two-faced, and neurotic, and should do something about it. Atmosphere: A curt, severe voice, surprising vehemence Stakes: A portrait of the castrating woman of the 1950s and of Rumaker's insecurity

The survivors choose change and consolidation: a switch to the quarter system in the fall of 1953; student fees cut nearly in half; the lower campus, from the dining hall to the Studies Building, is closed and then rented out (the end of a twenty-year tradition of communal meals), bringing the estimated operating budget down to $25,000 a year. The property remains the teachers', the emphasis remains on the individual and on closeness between student and teacher, and the arts remain at the center of the curriculum. Fees from $1,600 to $850; annual budget $25,000 Consequences: The college survives and takes a decisive turn toward the literary arts.

Back on a visit to assess the college's perilous situation and see what he could do, financially above all, with money from the family glove-making fortune. He teaches an informal architecture class that fall and organizes the circular-saw operation: every Saturday, early in the morning, everyone helps feed logs to the saw for the old coal stoves of the cottages that have them.

A group of young people traveling through the South asks to sleep on the grounds in their sleeping bags; everyone ends up in the kitchen talking. Merrill, back from Houston with Herb, is captivated by a dark-haired young man in a tight T-shirt and close-fitting Levi's, flattered and flirtatious. Merrill draws Rumaker near the door and orders him in a whisper to go and propose to the young man that he sleep with him; Rumaker refuses. A tight T-shirt, close-fitting Levi's; sleeping bags and a tent; whispers by the kitchen door Consequences: Merrill storms out; Rumaker dimly understands that he should leave, but stays

Back in New Haven in September 1953, Albers accepts an invitation received in Latin America: as a specialist in the State Department's international educational exchange program, he advises on the program of the brand-new Hochschule für Gestaltung in Ulm, on the Danube, halfway between Stuttgart and Munich. Consequences: Albers returns to Germany, twenty years after leaving in 1933

Lanier proposes an exhibition of four artist-craftsmen: Marguerite Wildenhain (pottery), Ida Dean (weaving), Merry Renk (jewelry), Ruth Asawa (baskets and wire sculpture); he would design the installation. He criticizes the “hodge-podge” of the big craft exhibitions, in which the individual work is lost for lack of space. Consequences: The exhibition is accepted by Morley.

A lively discussion in the kitchen; the flirtatious young man aims his remarks at Rumaker; Merrill, glued to him, lips parted, cheeks flushed, eyes shining; the visitors get up to go out; Merrill draws Rumaker near the door and whispers his order; refusal; the clinching argument of love; a second's hesitation; another whispered refusal; Merrill storms out; a night at Streamside, back to back Words: Merrill: “Go tell him I want to sleep with him.”; “If you really loved me you'd do it.”; Rumaker: “Merrill, I can't do that…”; “I can't.” Atmosphere: Fiercely urgent whispers, the beauty of the visitor, who toys with them by glancing over his shoulder Stakes: Rumaker reaches the limit of his submission; it sheds light on the couple's mechanism
